title: It’s David Hume’s world
gist: Reviewing a new two-volume edition of David Hume's essays, Jane O'Grady argues Hume straddled the Enlightenment and Counter-Enlightenment: his scepticism about causation, induction and the self, and his view of reason as a natural instinct subordinate to habit and emotion, anticipated Darwin, Freud and the 'masters of suspicion'. She credits him as an enduring model of philosophising but blames him for new 'superstitions' such as the scientisation of philosophy and default suspicion of our own minds.

insights.claim: O'Grady argues David Hume, while a key Enlightenment figure who attacked religious superstition, also straddles the Counter-Enlightenment by questioning reason's capacity for an impartial view of reality.
insights.so_what: Framing for long-run intellectual currents behind today's distrust of expertise and institutions.
insights.quote: Hume also straddles the Counter-Enlightenment, the backlash that began to demote reason
insights.locator: Yet, while he was a key figure
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: By blurring the line between humans and nature and treating reason as species-bound, Hume anticipated Darwin and influenced Paul Ricoeur's 'masters of suspicion' Nietzsche, Marx and Freud.
insights.so_what: Traces the genealogy of modern scepticism toward rational agency.
insights.locator: Yet, while he was a key figure
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: The new two-volume collection of Hume's essays has 28 index entries for the word 'superstition', reflecting his focus on reverence to priests as a curb on civil liberty.
insights.so_what: Illustrates Hume's core preoccupation with institutional authority and free thought.
insights.locator: The letter in which his fellow Scot
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: O'Grady contends Hume's contradictions are more fruitful than most of the 'pettifogging rigours' of analytic philosophy, making him an enduring model of how to philosophise.
insights.so_what: A critique of narrow technical rigour versus generative but inconsistent thinking.
insights.quote: He is not just a historical stepping stone, I’d argue, but an enduring model of how to philosophise.
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

themes.theme: Scepticism about causation, induction and self

insights.claim: Hume holds that repeated observation of 'constant conjunctions' gives no impression of necessary connection, so there is no rational basis for expecting past sequences to continue into the future.
insights.so_what: The problem of induction underlies every model that extrapolates from historical data.
insights.quote: “Your appeal to past experience decides nothing in the present case,” says Hume.
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: Hume argues there is no impression of an enduring self, so a person may be 'nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions'.
insights.so_what: Foundational idea for modern theories of mind and identity.
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: Hume's resolution is that nature and habit force us to believe in the world, causation and induction even though reason cannot justify them.
insights.so_what: Suggests practical belief and behaviour run on habit rather than justification, a basis for behavioural views of decision-making.
insights.quote: nature forces me to believe what reason would leave in suspense
insights.locator: He calls himself a mitigated sort
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: Hume sought to do for the mind what Newton did for physics, proposing resemblance, contiguity and cause and effect as the laws of association between ideas.
insights.so_what: An early mechanistic model of cognition that prefigures associative models of learning.
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: For Hume, belief is involuntary and is a species of sensation rather than a verdict of detached reason; one opinion simply 'strikes more strongly' than alternatives.
insights.so_what: Anticipates behavioural-economics views that conviction is felt, not reasoned.
insights.quote: “all probable reasoning is nothing but a species of sensation”
insights.locator: Hume seeks to chart the processes
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: Hume distinguishes slow, error-prone deliberative reason from fast, automatic 'experimental reasoning' shared with animals, and urges that the former be slave to the senses and emotions for survival.
insights.so_what: Mirrors modern dual-process (fast/slow) models of cognition.
insights.quote: “nothing but a species of instinct or mechanical power, that acts in us unknown to ourselves”
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: Hume's concept of 'sympathy', roughly modern empathy, is the mental mechanism he believes bridges the gap between 'is' and 'ought'.
insights.so_what: Grounds morality in emotional contagion rather than rational rules.
insights.locator: Similarly, although we have no impression
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: O'Grady argues Hume cheats by trading on the ambiguity of 'idea' as both mental event and subject matter, implicitly assuming the mind/matter distinction he claims to doubt.
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural flaw in empiricist theories of knowledge.
insights.locator: Hume is aware of the paradox
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: Norman Kemp Smith in 1905 and later New Humeans such as Galen Strawson argue Hume was a naturalist who may believe much of what he claims to doubt, rather than a nihilistic sceptic.
insights.so_what: Shows the shift in scholarly interpretation of Hume.
insights.locator: Hume has been, and still sometimes
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady

insights.claim: O'Grady concludes Hume initiated new superstitions of his own: the scientisation of philosophy, default suspicion of our world and minds, and the sophistry of literary theory.
insights.so_what: Argues modern cultural scepticism has Enlightenment roots that undermine shared trust.
insights.quote: an initiator of new ones—the scientisation of philosophy, default suspicion of our world and our minds
insights.locator: Hume has been, and still sometimes
insights.speaker: Jane O'Grady
